chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, and Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, all together from Ahmad ibn Al-Hasan Al-Mithammi, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about three partners, two testified against one. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Their testimony is not valid.'
ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of two partners against the third partner valid in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes a specific legal principle in Shia jurisprudence where the testimony of two partners against a third is deemed invalid, likely due to potential bias or conflict of interest inherent in their shared interest. It highlights the rigorous standards of evidence in commercial disputes, ensuring fairness by excluding those with direct stakes in the outcome. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on preventing injustice in financial transactions through precise evidentiary rules.

en.hubeali: Abu Ali Al Ashary, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, and Humeyd Bin Ziyad, from Al Hassan Bin Muhammad Bin Sama’at, both together from Ahmad Bin Al Hassan Al Maysami, from Aban Bin Usman, from Abdul Rahman Bin Abu Abdullah who said,
‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about three partners, two testified against one. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Both their testimonies are not allowed’.
en.sarwar: 1. Abu Ali al-Ash‘ariy has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa and Humayd ibn Ziyad from af-Hassan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama‘ah all from Ahmad ibn al-Hassan al-Mithamiy from Aban ibn ‘Uthman from ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn abu ‘Abd Allah who has narrated the following: “
I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of three partners of whom two have testified against one. He (the Imam) said, ‘Their testimony is not admissible. ’”
